Defendant: CHEN TING SAN DANIEL(陳定山) and LOONG SAN INVESTMENT COMPANY LIMITED (隆山置業有限公司), LEELOONG INVESTMENT COMPANY LIMITED (利隆置業有限公司) and LOONG WAN INVESTMENTS LIMITED (隆運置業有限公司)

facts.F1: The parties involved are family members, including Mr. Chen Tsing Kwan (the Father) and his four children, Daniel, Hepburn, TH and TN.
facts.F2: The Father founded the firm TK Chen & Associates and set up the three companies, Loong San, Leeloong, and Loong Wan, as corporate vehicles for investing in development projects and holding properties.
facts.F3: Daniel was entrusted with the daily management and financial affairs of the companies, and the Father's intention was that his children would be interested in the properties held by the companies in proportion to their shareholdings.
facts.F4: In 1996, the Father entrusted Daniel with the rentals collected by Leeloong to hold on trust for him, which was later extended to Loong San and Loong Wan.
facts.F5: Daniel refused to distribute the rentals to his siblings in 2010 and claimed the money as his own, alleging that the Father, his siblings, and the companies owed him money.
facts.F6: The Father asked Daniel to make available the books of accounts, records, and documents of the companies, which Daniel refused and removed all the documents from the registered office of the companies.
facts.F7: A forensic accountant was engaged to review the documents obtained by Hepburn and found that there was no concrete evidence to show the existence of the two loans to Loong San and Loong Wan as alleged by Daniel, and that Daniel had withdrawn a total of about HK$55,428,268 from Loong San and Loong Wan's bank accounts.
facts.F8: A director does not have to explain why the inspection is sought or demonstrate any particular ground or 'need to know' as a basis for inspection of company documents.
facts.F9: The person who asserts the director's intention to abuse confidence in relation to the company's affairs has the onus of establishing the claim and 'clear proof' is required to satisfy the court 'affirmatively' that the grant of the right of inspection would be detrimental to the interests of the company.

facts.F1: The plaintiffs obtained an order ex parte on 4 October 1996 restraining the 1st defendant from disposing or dealing with 770,469,230 shares in the 5th defendant.
facts.F2: The 1st plaintiff is a director of the 2nd plaintiff and owns 61% of the issued shares of the 2nd defendant, which is incorporated in Bermuda and quoted on the Alberta Stock Exchange.
facts.F3: The 2nd defendant owns 770,469,230 shares in the 5th defendant, which is listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, and these shares are subject to a pledge in favour of the 1st defendant.
facts.F4: A board meeting of the 2nd defendant on 28 August 1996 resolved to sell the 2nd defendant's shares in the 5th defendant.
facts.F5: The 4th defendant offered to buy the Seaunion shares at a price of HK$0.13 per share, with a deposit of HK$5,000,000 and payment of HK$55,000,000 within 60 days.
facts.F6: The offer was accepted by Mr Nightingale on behalf of the 2nd defendant.
facts.F7: The 2nd defendant's shares in the 5th defendant had a trading history showing a price of 13.5 cents on 28 August and a rise to about 30 cents per share on 4 October 1996.

facts.F9: The 2nd plaintiff holds 53,953,698 shares (69.61%) in the 2nd defendant.
facts.F10: There are allegations of Mr Wong being closely related to the 4th defendant, which he denies.

claim: Tunlees claims against Master for the return of the $130,000.00 deposit as well as loss of profit and damages in excess of $600,000.00
requested_remedy: Tunlees claims against Master for the return of the $130,000.00 deposit as well as loss of profit and damages in excess of $600,000.00
parties: Plaintiff: TUNLEES WATCH MFG. (HK) CO. LIMITED
Defendant: CHANG HOK MAN STEPHEN trading as MASTER INTERNATIONAL COMPANY

facts.F1: Tunlees Watch MFG. (HK) CO. Limited (Tunlees) and the defendant Chang Hok Man Stephen trading as Master International Company (Master) entered an exclusive distributorship agreement on 22 March 1997.
facts.F2: Under the agreement, Master appointed Tunlees as its exclusive distributor for Master Image Gravers I, II, and III and other optional accessories in the United Arab Emirates (U.A.E.) for two years.
facts.F3: Tunlees paid Master a deposit of $130,000.00, initially for a Graver I, but later asked to exchange it for a Graver III, which was never delivered.
facts.F4: Tunlees had procured purchase orders for 9 sets of Graver III, but Master failed to supply them.
facts.F5: Master approached Emirate Jewellery Department Store (EJDS) directly with a quotation, breaching clause 9 of the agreement, which required Master to refer all U.A.E. enquiries to Tunlees.
facts.F6: Tunlees claims Master repudiated the agreement.
facts.F7: Master counterclaims that Tunlees failed to devote its best efforts to provide and maintain competent and aggressive solicitation for the sale of the products and that Tunlees informed Master it was no longer interested in carrying out the agreement.
facts.F8: Master denies making any representation or warranty about the availability of Graver III by the end of June 1997.
facts.F9: Tunlees and EJDS had an agreement for the purchase of 6 sets of Graver III with delivery dates commencing before the end of August 1997, but Master’s failure to deliver led to the cancellation of this agreement.
facts.F10: EJDS directly contacted Master and expressed interest in purchasing Graver III, leading to a quotation from Master.
facts.F11: Master and EJDS entered into a deal for the supply of Graver III at a lower price than that offered to Tunlees.
facts.F12: Tunlees was required to purchase at least 3 sets of Graver III by 21 September 1997.
facts.F13: Tunlees incurred air-ticket expenses of HK$6,820.00.

reference_issues: Whether Master’s conduct constituted a breach of the agreement.
Whether Master repudiated the agreement.
Whether Tunlees can claim damages, including loss of profit.
